title: Treaties & International Law
hook: If no world government can pass laws, how do nations bind themselves at all? Largely by agreeing to — treaties are the contracts that knit the international order together.
key_points: International law is the body of rules governing relations between states.
Treaties are binding agreements states consent to — the main source of that law.
It rests heavily on consent: states are generally bound by what they agree to.
Enforcement is the weak point — there is no global police, so compliance leans on reciprocity and reputation.
content_html: If the international system has no government above states, how can there be law between them at all? The answer is that international law works differently from domestic law: it is built largely on agreement rather than command. International law is the body of rules governing relations among states, and its most important source is the treaty — a binding agreement that states voluntarily enter into, ranging from a trade deal between two countries to a global convention signed by nearly all of them.
extra_html: The defining principle is consent. Because states are sovereign, they are generally bound only by rules they have agreed to, which is why so much of international law takes the form of treaties a state chooses to ratify. (Some rules, like the prohibition on genocide, are treated as binding on all states regardless of consent, but these are the exception.) Encyclopaedia Britannica notes that this consent-based foundation gives international law real force in everyday matters — trade, diplomacy, shipping, communications — where predictable rules serve everyone's interest. The persistent weakness is enforcement. There is no global police force or compulsory court to make a powerful state comply if it chooses not to, so international law leans on softer mechanisms: reciprocity (breaking a rule invites others to break it too), reputation and the value of being seen as reliable, diplomatic and economic pressure, and the work of international bodies. This is why international law is often followed far more than its skeptics expect, yet can be flouted by states willing to bear the costs — a tension that runs through the whole field.

related.title: Sovereignty Among Nations
related.hook: Inside its borders a state is supreme — but in the world of states there's no higher ruler. That gap, called anarchy, shapes everything about international politics.

related.title: The UN & International Organizations
related.hook: Sovereign states that answer to no one above them still build standing clubs to cooperate. The UN is the largest — a forum, not a world government.

related.title: The Rule of Law
related.hook: The principle that everyone — including those in power — is bound by the same publicly known laws, applied equally.

flashcards.back_html: A binding agreement between states that they consent to — the main source of international law.

flashcards.prompt: International law rests heavily on which principle?

choices.text: Consent — states are generally bound by what they agree to
Majority vote of the world's population
Decrees from a single global ruler

flashcards.explanation_html: Without a world legislature, states are mostly bound by rules they have consented to, especially through treaties.

flashcards.prompt: What is the weakest link in international law compared with domestic law?

choices.text: Enforcement — there is no global police to compel compliance
Getting any state to ever agree to anything

flashcards.explanation_html: The rules exist and are often followed, but with no global enforcer, compliance leans on reciprocity, reputation, and pressure rather than coercion.
